teaser: The night Britain's Parliament burned down, Turner was in the crowd with a sketchbook.
review_notes:
The twin towers in the flames (about 0.27, 0.44) are identified as Westminster Abbey; please confirm against the Cleveland Museum's description.
The crowd applauding when a roof fell in is reported in contemporary accounts.
The varnishing-day story (Rippingille's account) concerns the other version, now in Philadelphia, shown at the British Institution in early 1835; the text says so.
Constable sketching the fire from a cab on Westminster Bridge.
Whether Turner watched from a hired boat is traditional and stated as “probably.”

lesson.text: The stars are out. You can count a few of them in the top right corner, white points in a dark blue sky. So it is night. Yet the left half of this picture is brighter than any noon, and a stone bridge on the right glows like the inside of a lamp. Turner painted an evening when London had two skies at once.

The date was October 16, 1834. Around six in the evening, fire broke out in the Palace of Westminster, the rambling medieval complex where Britain's two houses of Parliament met: the Lords and the Commons. By midnight most of it was gone.

The cause was paperwork. For centuries the Treasury had kept accounts on notched wooden sticks called tallies. Workmen were told to burn two cartloads of the obsolete sticks in the furnaces under the House of Lords. The flues overheated, and the government burned down its own home.

Tens of thousands of Londoners poured out to watch. They filled the riverbanks, the bridges and every boat that could be hired. Turner, 59 years old, was among them, moving from spot to spot and probably taking to the water as well. He filled sketchbook pages that night, then built two large oil paintings from them. This is the second.

lesson.title: Where the light goes
lesson.text: The fire sits far away on the opposite bank. Follow its light as it crosses the river.

spots.title: The blaze
spots.text: Pure yellow and white paint, laid on thick. There are no drawn flames, only a wall of light. Turner paints the fire by painting brightness itself.

spots.title: Towers in the furnace
spots.text: Two pale Gothic towers stand in the glow, most likely those of Westminster Abbey next door. They are the only crisp architecture left on that bank.

spots.title: The river on fire
spots.text: The Thames repeats the blaze in long gold streaks. Small dark boats crowd the water, their passengers black against the reflection.

spots.title: The bridge
spots.text: Westminster Bridge rears up like a white cliff and seems to melt toward the fire at its far end. Turner made it much taller and paler than it was.

lesson.text: That bridge is the strangest thing here. Stone should be the most solid object in view, but it looks weightless, almost transparent, while the fire across the water looks dense enough to touch. Turner swaps their natures. Along the top of the bridge, the parapet is packed with a frieze of tiny heads.
The same is true along the whole bottom edge of the canvas. We stand on the south bank behind a mass of onlookers, shoulder to shoulder in the dark. Half the subject of the painting is the audience.

Many in the crowd were not sorry. Parliament was unpopular with the poor after a harsh new welfare law passed that year. Witnesses reported that when one of the roofs crashed in, a section of the crowd clapped, as if at a theater.

And Turner stages it like theater: spotlit set at the back, audience in shadow at the front. But he also keeps the cool, indifferent night in view. One thing in the sky belongs to the fire, and another belongs to the night. They are easy to confuse.
Orange sparks blow across the top of the picture. Where do they give way to real stars?

spots.title: Stars
spots.text: In the deep blue-green corner, white dots shine steadily. To their left, the specks are orange and ragged: burning debris carried on the wind. Fire and starlight meet in one sky.

lesson.text: The wind matters. It pushes the smoke in a great gray wing from the fire toward the bridge, so the canvas reads from left to right: heat, then smoke, then cold stone and stars. Turner uses only two families of color for this, hot yellows and oranges against cool blues and violets, and lets them collide in the middle.
Turner treats a national disaster as a spectacle of light. The buildings barely appear. Fire, water, smoke and air do the talking.

The first version of the subject, now in Philadelphia, has a legend of its own. A fellow painter recalled that Turner sent it to the gallery as a blur of color, then painted most of it on the wall in a few hours while other artists watched, and walked off without stepping back to check it.

He was not the only painter out that night. John Constable, his great rival in landscape, watched from a cab on Westminster Bridge and drew the scene for his family. Only Turner turned it into paintings this size, about 92 by 123 cm (3 by 4 feet).

spots.title: The near crowd
spots.text: Dark heads and shoulders, a few faces catching the orange light. Turner sketches them in quick, soft strokes. They are a mass, not portraits.

spots.title: A street lamp
spots.text: A small lamp on a post burns white at the water's edge. Next to the fire, its light is almost a joke.

spots.title: Spectators on the bridge
spots.text: A dotted line of heads runs along the parapet, with lamps glowing above. The whole bridge has become a grandstand.

spots.title: Packed against the arch
spots.text: More onlookers jam the bank under the bridge, a mound of faces lit pink and yellow by a fire far across the water.

spots.title: The smoke
spots.text: A dark gray plume leans to the right, pushed by the wind. Its edge is the border between the hot half of the picture and the cold half.

spots.title: Flying embers
spots.text: Flecks of orange paint arc across the top of the canvas. The dabs are thick enough to sit raised on the surface, like real cinders.

lesson.text: From the ashes came the building the world now pictures when it thinks of London. A new Palace of Westminster rose on the site over the next three decades, with its famous clock tower. The Parliament on the postcards exists because of the night Turner painted.

quiz.question: What started the fire of 1834?
options: Burning old wooden tally sticks in the furnaces
A candle left in the library
quiz.explanation: Workmen burned two cartloads of obsolete tally sticks and the flues overheated.

quiz.question: How does Turner paint the stone bridge?
options: Dark and heavy, blocking the view
quiz.explanation: The bridge looks like a glowing white cliff that melts toward the fire.

quiz.question: What can you find in the top right corner of the sky?
quiz.explanation: White stars shine in the dark blue corner, beyond the orange sparks.

quiz.question: Where does the viewer stand in the painting?
options: Behind a crowd on the bank across the river
On the deck of a fire boat
quiz.explanation: We look over the heads of onlookers on the opposite bank.

quiz.question: Which direction does the wind push the smoke in the picture?
options: From the fire toward the bridge, left to right
quiz.explanation: A gray wing of smoke leans from the fire on the left toward the bridge on the right.

facts.text: Turner painted only one picture of the fire.
facts.explanation: He made two large oil paintings; this is the second, and the first is in Philadelphia.

facts.text: Turner was present in London on the night of the fire and sketched it.
facts.explanation: He was in the crowd and filled sketchbook pages that night.

facts.text: The whole crowd watched the fire in horrified silence.
facts.explanation: Witnesses reported that some people applauded when a roof fell in.
